This diagram illustrates three methods for handling user data deletion requests in machine learning systems, comparing their computational costs. At the top, a user submits a deletion request for sensitive private information, which triggers a process in the Model Provider that involves training a CLM (Continual Learning Model) from a dataset. The diagram then presents three distinct approaches: (a) Data De-duplication, which removes duplicate data and re-trains the model, requiring approximately 900 A100 GPU days; (b) Differential Privacy, which adds noise to the training process and re-trains the model, requiring approximately 1800 A100 GPU days; and (c) Machine Unlearning, which uses gradient ascent to modify the model directly without retraining, requiring only approximately 0.001 A100 GPU days. The key finding is that machine unlearning is dramatically more computationally efficient than the other two methods for performing model updates in response to deletion requests.

Section (b) shows a process called "Differential Privacy", which involves adding noise to the training data and retraining the model, requiring approximately 1800 A100 GPU days. Section (c) shows a process called "Machine Unlearning", which involves modifying the model to remove user data, requiring approximately 0.001 A100 GPU days. 

The diagram illustrates the trade-offs between these methods in terms of computational cost and model accuracy.

This figure is a diagram illustrating a knowledge distillation framework, comparing student and teacher model architectures and detailing four types of knowledge transfer losses. The key finding is that these methods progressively transfer knowledge from a complex teacher to a simpler student by aligning outputs, feature maps, and relational structures across multiple levels.

This is a flowchart illustrating an automated software refactoring system. The process begins with a Java source file, which triggers a context-aware planner agent to gather context (dependent classes, quality metrics, and source code). This context is then used by a refactoring generator agent to produce a refactored version of the target class. The refactored code is compiled and tested in an iterative loop—up to 20 times—if compilation or testing fails, the system returns to the refactoring agent for a new attempt. If all tests pass after 20 iterations, the refactored code is kept; otherwise, the original code is retained. The diagram shows a clear feedback loop between refactoring, compilation, and testing, with conditional branching based on success or failure.
